newsitem.title: NORWAY: Portugal upset by Statoil exploration off E.Timor.
newsitem.headline: Portugal upset by Statoil exploration off E.Timor.

text.p: Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said on Tuesday his country would complain to the United Nations over exploration by state-owned Norwegian oil company Statoil in a legally grey zone in the Timor Sea, the Norwegian NTB news agency reported.
Guterres said during talks in Oslo with his Norwegian counterpart Thorbjoern Jagland that Statoil's exploration activities in the region were unlawful, NTB said.

Statoil public affairs manager Kai Nielsen said the company operated as any other commercial firm. "There are other licence groups there, living with the same terms. If Portugal wants to protest, it should go to Australia and Indonesia, not to the oil companies or the Prime Minister of Norway," he added.
The Portuguese premier was in the Norwegian capital on an unofficial visit to attend the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize ceremony.

The prize went jointly to human rights campaigner Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo and resistance leader Jose Ramos Horta in recognition of their work to find a peaceful solution to the conflict in East Timor.

The former Portuguese colony has been in turmoil since Indonesia invaded it in 1975 and annexed it the following year. The U.N. has never recognised Indonesia's claims to the island and still accepts Portugal to be its administrative power.
Statoil, or Den norske stats oljeselskap AS, took a 25 percent stake in July in an offshore exploration licence in a Zone of Cooperation between Indonesia and Australia.
Exploration drilling is due to begin in February. The agreement between Indonesia and Australia means that any resources discovered would be shared equally between the two.

Mobil Oil of the United States is operator of the licence with 25 percent. Other partners are Royal Dutch/Shell with 25 percent, Hardy Oil and Gas Plc with 13 percent and Mitsubishi Oil Co of Japan with 12 percent.

NTB said the Jagland had not accepted the Portuguese complaint. "Norwegian authorities are sure that Statoil's activities are not in conflict with international law," NTB quoted Jagland as saying after talks.

"It is clearly a commercial activity and cannot be seen as Norwegian recognition of Indonesia's occupation of East Timor. Norway's policy is clear: We have never and will never recognise Indonesia's annexation of East Timor."

But Guterres said: "We think the agreement between Indonesia and Australia over this stretch of sea is illegal. All activities under this agreement are thereby illegal according to international law."
He said Portugal would take up the matter at the U.N. in connection with talks on human rights and self-determination for the East Timorese people, according to NTB.
